1.answer: Adding an item: work out its k positions using the k hash functions (each taken modulo m) and set all of those bits to 1. A bit that is already 1 stays 1. Looking an item up: work out the same k positions and look at those bits. If any of them is 0, the item was definitely never added. If all of them are 1, the item was probably added.
1.quote: Add an item: compute its k positions and set all of those bits to 1. (If a bit is already 1, it stays 1.)

2.answer: It can give false positives: it says "probably yes" for an item that was never added, because other items happened to set all of that item's bits. It can never give a false negative. Adding an item sets its bits to 1, and bits never go back to 0, so an item that was added always finds all its bits set.
2.quote: If any of them is 0, the item was definitely never added. Adding it would have set that bit to 1, and bits never go back to 0.

3.answer: Other items may share those bits. Setting them back to 0 could erase bits that other items depend on, and those items would then get false negatives. A counting Bloom filter, which keeps a counter in each slot, can delete.
3.quote: Setting an item's bits back to 0 might erase bits that other items also depend on, and then those items would get false negatives.

4.answer: It says "probably yes", which is a false positive. Whatever positions the item hashes to, all of them are 1, so the check finds no 0. The page's own estimate agrees: with f = 1, the false positive rate f^k comes to 100%. The page never mentions this case directly; this is reasoned from the check rule.
4.quote: If all of them are 1, the item was probably added. Those bits might have been set by other items.
